archetype.name: Pretender (goalie-propped)
archetype.definition: A San Jose team whose near-.500 record and spot in the soft Pacific race rest on above-expected goaltending and close-game points, not on how it plays at 5-on-5.

report.headline: Celebrini and the goalies keep a badly out-chanced team near .500
report.take:
San Jose sits fourth in a weak Pacific at 11-12-2, 19th of 32 on the site, and the record flatters the team underneath it. The Sharks have been outscored 89-69, a goal differential per game that ranks 28th. At 5-on-5 they own only a 43.7% share of the expected goals, 30th in the league. They also give up 30.4 shots a game, 31st. This is a team that spends most nights defending.

Two things keep the standings respectable. The first is goaltending: the goalies are 7.8 goals saved above expected, seventh in the league, after sinking the club at -25.7 last season. Alex Nedeljkovic has done most of that work (+7.1 in nine starts against Yaroslav Askarov's +2.1 in 16). The second is Macklin Celebrini: 29 points in 23 games, 12 of them on the power play, second on the centers' tab. His line wins its minutes, with a 51.3% expected-goals share on a team at 43.7%. The forward group's A+ grade is essentially his grade.

The numbers hide a split verdict on luck. Pts vs Goal Diff is +2.4, sixth in the league, and it was +6.1 last year, so the Sharks have now banked extra points from close games two seasons running. That tends not to hold. Yet the 5-on-5 PDO is 98.1, below average, so the even-strength percentages are not inflated. The real problem is the process. The 43.7% expected-goals share matches the 2024-25 team that finished 32nd and is worse than last season's 47.6%. The defense also bleeds production to opposing wingers: 0.78 points a game, last in the league.

Where it goes from here depends on whether the goaltending holds. The pace says 79 points, short of last year's 86. A last-five run of 3-1-1 came with an even goal differential and several overtime results, so it is noise more than a turn. Without a real change in shot share, this projects as a lottery-range team with a star center, not a playoff climber.

strengths.title: Celebrini carries the offense
strengths.body: Celebrini has 29 points in 23 games and plays nearly 23 minutes a night. His 51.3% expected-goals share stands out on a team that sits at 43.7%. He is the one forward the sheet lists, so the A+ forward grade is effectively his. That is real and should last, but it is a one-man case.

strengths.title: Goaltending above expected
strengths.body: The goalies are +7.8 GSAx, seventh in the league, a sharp reversal from -25.7 last season. Nedeljkovic's .902 and +7.1 lead the way, while Askarov has the larger share of starts at a lesser .888. Some of this is skill, but it is the piece most likely to slip under 30-plus shots a night.

concerns.title: Out-chanced almost every night
concerns.body: A 43.7% expected-goals share ranks 30th and is worse than last season's 47.6%. The 30.4 shots allowed a game rank 31st. Goals allowed per game are worse than the league by 0.36, and the goalies are already above expected. This is the root of the -20 differential, and nothing in the sheet suggests it is improving.

concerns.title: Wingers run free against them
concerns.body: Opposing wingers score 0.78 points a game against San Jose, the worst mark in the league. Wingers take 58.1% of the points scored against the Sharks, against a league norm of 43%. Defensemen are well contained (fifth), so the leak is in forward coverage on the flanks rather than the point.

concerns.title: Close-game points won't last
concerns.body: Pts vs Goal Diff of +2.4 ranks sixth, following +6.1 last year. The last five games went 3-1-1 with a 0 differential, which is points without margin. Expect the record to drift toward what a -0.8 goal differential per game implies.

trend.note: October and November look alike at both ends: under three goals scored and around three and a half allowed per game. The recent 3-1-1 came on an even goal differential, while the last ten were -9, so nothing structural has turned.

weekAhead.headline: Three top-eight teams around a winnable trip to Anaheim
weekAhead.body:
Four games, three of them against teams in the site's top eight. It opens at home against Minnesota (17-3-5, second on the site), which allows the fewest goals in the league behind goalies who lead it at +16.2 GSAx. Then comes a trip to Anaheim (11-12-1), the week's best chance: the Ducks' goalies stop .858, last in the league.

The week closes with a back-to-back: Vegas at home, then at Colorado. Both control play at 5-on-5, with Vegas at a 53.3% expected-goals share and Colorado at 53% of shot attempts. That is a bad matchup for a team that already allows 30.4 shots a night. Two to four points would be a fair result.

keyMatchups.title: Sharks PK vs Anaheim's power play
keyMatchups.body: Anaheim converts 34.2% of its power plays, first in the league. San Jose kills only 73.9%, 21st. The Ducks' goaltending (.858) makes this a game the Sharks can win, but only if they stay out of the box.

keyMatchups.title: Celebrini against Minnesota's center gap
keyMatchups.body: Minnesota allows 0.5 points a game to centers, 30th in the league, and centers take half the points scored against it. That is exactly Celebrini's lane. The catch is the Wild's .916 team save percentage, second in the league.

keyMatchups.title: Back-to-back vs possession teams
keyMatchups.body: Vegas (53.3% xGF) and Colorado (53% CF, second in offense) on consecutive days will test a team that lives in its own end. Expect the goalies' workload to decide both games more than San Jose's attack.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts the back-to-back, and whether Nedeljkovic's above-expected saves hold up against Vegas and Colorado shot volume.

restOfSeason.body:
The sustainable parts are Celebrini and a goaltending tandem that is at least competent. The unsustainable parts are a +2.4 Pts vs Goal Diff and goalies working well above expected behind a 30th-ranked expected-goals share. The 5-on-5 PDO of 98.1 suggests even-strength shooting could tick up a little. That will not offset the shot deficit or the 73.9% penalty kill.

The current pace is 79 points. I expect a bit less, roughly 72 to 80 points and 33 to 36 wins, as close-game luck evens out. The weak Pacific keeps them nominally in the race for a while, but the play points to the lower half of the conference.
swingFactors: Whether Nedeljkovic and Askarov stay above expected under 30-plus shots a night
Any improvement in 5-on-5 shot and chance share

confidence.note: 25 games; the shot-share signal is consistent with history, but the goaltending sample is small.
